result.summary: This section is a single note by Proclus about the lost poem Divination by Birds. It reports that some editors placed the poem after line 828 of Hesiod's Works and Days, while Apollonius of Rhodes rejected it as spurious.

scenes.title: Proclus on a disputed poem
scenes.summary: Proclus notes that some editors attach the Divination by Birds to the end of Works and Days, though Apollonius of Rhodes rejected it as spurious.

characters.name: Proclus
characters.description: ancient commentator on Hesiod's Works and Days

characters.name: Apollonius of Rhodes
characters.description: scholar-poet who rejected the Divination by Birds as spurious

analysis.text: The note shows how ancient scholars debated which poems truly belonged to Hesiod. Judgements of authenticity, such as that of Apollonius, shaped which texts were copied and handed down.
Bird divination suits the practical, omen-minded outlook of Works and Days, which explains why some editors appended such a poem to it.

fun_facts.text: Apollonius of Rhodes, known for the Argonautica, also served as head of the Library of Alexandria, so his views on authenticity carried weight.

language_notes.text: "Follow this verse" means the poem is placed immediately after line 828, so it would continue, and effectively conclude, Works and Days.
"Spurious" means not genuinely by Hesiod; Apollonius judged the poem a false attribution.

context_notes.text: Proclus was a later ancient commentator on Hesiod. Apollonius of Rhodes, a Hellenistic scholar-poet and librarian at Alexandria, is known for the Argonautica and for judging authenticity.
